title: Clootie Dumpling
subtitle: Scottish boiled fruit pudding wrapped in a cloth
excerpt: A Scottish tradition of boiling a spiced fruit-and-suet dough inside a floured cloth, giving the finished pudding a distinctive firm skin on the outside and a dense, dark, sweet interior.
sourceNotes: A Scottish tradition documented since at least the 18th century. The cloth (called a cloot in Scots) creates the characteristic dry skin unique to this pudding. Traditionally served on birthdays and at Hogmanay as well as Christmas, with small silver coins or charms stirred into the mixture as tokens of fortune.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in slices once cooled and the skin has set. Thaw overnight in the fridge. Reheat by steaming for 20 minutes, or slice and fry in butter until hot through.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The dumpling keeps well for 5 days in the fridge and actually improves over the first 2 days as the skin firms further.
recipe.temperatureNote: for drying the skin after boiling

content.text: Clootie dumpling is a Scottish boiled fruit pudding cooked inside a damp, floured cloth, the cloot, which gives its outside a characteristic dry, slightly papery skin that is quite unlike any other pudding. Inside it is dense, dark, and sweet with dried fruit and warm spice. Boil for 2.5 to 3 hours, then dry the skin briefly in the oven before serving.

items.prepNote: plus extra for dusting the cloth

content.text: In a large bowl, combine the flour, oats, suet, sugar, currants, sultanas, spices, and bicarbonate of soda. Make a well in the centre. Add the treacle, beaten egg, and most of the milk. Mix to a thick, sticky dough, adding the remaining milk if needed to bring it together. The dough should be firm enough to hold its shape but moist throughout.

You need a large square of plain cotton or linen cloth, at least 60cm square, an old tea towel or pillowcase works well. Dip the cloth in boiling water, then squeeze out as much water as you can. Spread it out on a surface and dust the centre generously with flour, shaking off the excess. The flour creates the skin.

Pile the dough into the centre of the cloth. Bring the four corners up and over the dough. Gather the cloth tightly around the dough and tie it securely with string, leaving a generous 5cm of space between the knot and the top of the dough, the dumpling will expand during boiling and needs room.

Lower the dumpling into a large pan of boiling water. Place an upturned saucer or trivet in the bottom of the pan first so the dumpling does not sit directly on the base. The knot end should stay above the waterline. Cover the pan and boil steadily over a medium heat for 2.5 to 3 hours, checking every 30 minutes and topping up with boiling water to keep the dumpling submerged.

Lift the dumpling from the pan and place it in a colander over the sink. Carefully peel away the cloth, it should come away cleanly if the flour coating worked. Place the dumpling on a baking tray and put it in a 150°C oven for 15 to 20 minutes until the skin dries to a slightly glossy, dark finish. Serve in slices with custard or cream.

items.symptom: The skin is wet and sticks to the cloth
items.cause: The cloth was not hot enough, not dusted well enough with flour, or the oven-drying step was skipped.
items.fix: Dip the cloth in truly boiling water, then flour it generously. Always dry the dumpling in the oven after unwrapping, the oven step is not optional.

items.cause: The cloth was tied too tightly, leaving no room for expansion.
items.fix: Always leave a clear 5cm between the knot and the top of the dough. The mixture expands considerably during the long boil.

items.symptom: The dumpling tastes bland or under-sweet
items.cause: Light muscovado or ordinary brown sugar was used instead of dark muscovado.
items.fix: Dark muscovado and black treacle together give the characteristic deep flavour. Light muscovado makes a noticeably less complex pudding.

content.text: Keeps in the fridge, wrapped, for 5 days. The flavour improves over the first 2 days. Reheat by steaming slices for 20 minutes, or slice and fry in butter over a medium heat until hot and slightly caramelised at the edges, the traditional breakfast method.
